justification: The article’s spine is the step-down and the impossibility of proving it: “The maneuver is the cheap part … It was always going to be the cheap part,” followed by a whole closing section on how “a success looks like an empty picture. So does a forecast that was wrong, and a contrail too thin to register, and a sheet of cloud sitting over the top of one.” That is B. A (humidity forecasting) and C (crystal growth) are supporting paragraphs subordinate to that argument, and D’s comparison of contrail warming against fuel warming is never made anywhere in the text.

Both attributes are stated: “the layer runs a couple of hundred miles with a depth that would fit inside a small hill,” confirmed by Vestrigg’s “The layers are usually shallow enough that one step down is out of them,” and “Air can sit well past ice saturation and make no cloud of its own … So the sky stays clear.” That is A. B is contradicted by that same no-cloud sentence; C is contradicted by “a layer like that has nothing in it to look at” and “the first anyone knows of it is the mark an airplane leaves crossing it”; D attributes to the layer what the text says of the contrail, which needs time “to spread wide enough for a satellite to register it.”

The reason given for the night-only rule is the missing daytime counterweight: “a spreading contrail holds in heat that would otherwise leave, and in daylight it also turns some sunlight back toward space, so the two effects pull against one another, while after dark there is nothing pulling the other way.” That is D. C overstates the same sentence — daylight only means the two effects oppose each other, not that a contrail cools on balance. A (light night traffic) and B (deeper layers at night) are never asserted; the text says only that the layers are shallow.

The untouched flights are the calibration: “Of 141 flights that were left alone and flew straight through a forecast layer, 61 left a mark anybody could find afterward. The forecast was calling for wet air a good deal more often than the sky supplied it.” If well under half of forecast layers actually produce a contrail, then many of the 96 descents that were flown avoided nothing — C. A misreads the construction: all 141 flew through a forecast layer by definition; B inverts the direction of the error (over-calling, not missing); D is contradicted by the 61 that did leave a mark.

The writer ranks the two sources explicitly: “the satellite count is the smallest thing those two winters produced … the findings that will outlast the trial are his … The second of those comes off records the center already keeps and needed no picture at all.” That is A. C is contradicted by that ranking; D overstates it, since “A picture that shows a contrail settles that one flight” and no call is made to stop the imagery; B misassigns Vestrigg’s wish to the writer, who answers it with the noncommittal “Perhaps it would.”

The article's spine is a cheap operational fix and the impossibility of proving it worked: the trial flies "two thousand feet beneath" the layer, "An adjusted airplane burned about two percent more" and "The maneuver is the cheap part", after which "Which leaves the counting" opens a whole closing section on why "An empty one settles nothing." That is B. A and C are the setup, not the subject — the humidity-forecast weakness and the crystal physics each occupy a single early paragraph and exist to explain why the maneuver was tried. D is never addressed: the text quantifies fuel burn and contrail counts but never compares aviation's cloud warming with its combustion warming.

Both halves of A are stated: "a layer like that has nothing in it to look at. Air can sit well past ice saturation and make no cloud of its own", and "the layer runs a couple of hundred miles with a depth that would fit inside a small hill", confirmed by Vestrigg's "The layers are usually shallow enough that one step down is out of them." B is the direct opposite — "the sky stays clear" precisely because "starting a crystal from nothing needs roughly half again as much vapor as keeping an existing one alive". C fails for the same reason: "the first anyone knows of it is the mark an airplane leaves crossing it", so no crew can pick one out. D transfers a property of the contrail ("a spreading contrail", "it needs anywhere from five minutes to an hour to spread") onto the layer, which the text never describes as spreading.

The reason given is the absence of any offsetting effect after dark: "a spreading contrail holds in heat that would otherwise leave, and in daylight it also turns some sunlight back toward space, so the two effects pull against one another, while after dark there is nothing pulling the other way." That is D. C overreads the same sentence: daylight only means the two effects oppose each other, never that a daytime contrail nets out as cooling. A is unsupported and cuts against "On a busy evening four or five tracks cross the same square of sky"; the descents were in fact lost to traffic and other pressures ("the rest were traded away for traffic, for weather, for a crew that wanted the fuel"). B invents a night/day difference in layer depth; depth is described once, generically, as shallow.

The untouched flights are the control group, and their result is a false-alarm rate: "Of 141 flights that were left alone and flew straight through a forecast layer, 61 left a mark anybody could find afterward. The forecast was calling for wet air a good deal more often than the sky supplied it." If well under half of forecast layers produce a contrail, then descents ordered off that same forecast are mostly avoiding nothing — which the close makes explicit as a durable finding, "that the forecast asks for more descents than the sky calls for". That is C. A misreads the denominator: all 141 flew straight through a forecast layer; it is the marks, not the layers, that number fewer than half. B reverses the direction of the error — the forecast over-calls wet air, it does not miss it. D is contradicted outright by the 61 flights that did leave a mark.

The writer ranks the imagery below the center's paperwork: "the satellite count is the smallest thing those two winters produced", the lasting findings are Colverdine's, and "The second of those comes off records the center already keeps and needed no picture at all." That is A. C is contradicted by that explicit ranking — he does not hold the two kinds of evidence level. D overstates in the other direction: "A picture that shows a contrail settles that one flight", so the imagery is granted real if narrow value, and he never proposes stopping it ("A third winter is being flown"). B attributes Vestrigg's hope to the writer, who answers it with the flat hedge "Perhaps it would" and the closing "The sensors have not been fitted."

findings.quote: They are shallow, and they hold no cloud.
findings.note: WORLD_KNOWLEDGE (blind pick A). Domain knowledge of ice-supersaturated regions -- they are geometrically thin and can be entirely clear of cloud, and are invisible from the flight deck -- decides this without the passage; C is the standard misconception and D describes contrail spreading rather than the layers. The distractors are substantive positions, so this is normal test design routed to adjudication, not a form leak.

findings.quote: After dark nothing works against the warming, since no sunlight is turned away.
findings.note: WORLD_KNOWLEDGE (blind pick D). The day/night contrail asymmetry (no shortwave albedo offset at night) is a well-known result in the field; a solver who knows it picks D and reads C as the overstated version of the same idea. A and B remain substantive operational rationales for a night-only trial, so the passage is still needed to confirm -- flag, not kill.

findings.quote: He regards the imagery as worthless and would put an end to it.
findings.note: PARTIALLY. Two options fall to form alone with no domain knowledge: D is the extreme-language option ('worthless', 'put an end to it') and C is the no-preference neutrality option, which the stem's presupposition of an attitude already disfavours. That halves the field to A/B passage-blind; A vs B genuinely needs the text.

findings.quote: It is fixed hard into the stone so that the leaf cannot move once the water rises.
findings.note: PARTIALLY (blind lean A). B is self-defeating on its face -- a pin that a leaf stands and swings on cannot be the thing that prevents the leaf moving -- and D overreaches with 'the whole of the water's push' and 'every leaf'. Both go without any domain knowledge, leaving A vs C, which the passage must still decide.

findings.quote: Because the plant was valued on its own, what a buyer paid turned mainly on the debts against the houses.
findings.note: PARTIALLY. B is eliminable blind as a category confusion (houses on a milk round do not carry debts against them) and D ends in a town-wide milk-price conclusion the stem does not ask about; neither elimination needs domain knowledge. A and C both stay live, so the passage is still required to choose.

findings.quote: Verkan var ungefär densamma, och badet krävde varken nytt avtal eller längre transport.
findings.note: PARTIALLY (blind lean A). D contradicts the stem's presupposition that the factory faced a live choice between two workable options, and A has the canonical key shape for a 'why choose X over Y' item -- comparable effect plus practical convenience. C is nevertheless a substantive rival on the size of the difference, so the passage still decides A vs C; not a kill.

findings.quote: Efterglöden var den svåraste tekniska frågan i hela tändsticksindustrin.
findings.note: PARTIALLY (blind lean C). Two options fall to form alone: A carries an industry-wide superlative that no single-factory text could support, and B a universal quantifier ('varje förändring'). That leaves the balanced two-factor C against the reductive monocausal D, and test-wiseness favours C -- materially better than chance, but D stays substantive enough that this is a flag rather than a structural-leak kill.

findings.quote: Häftena kan knappast säga något om hur planscherna faktiskt användes i klassrummen.
findings.note: PARTIALLY (blind lean A). D is pragmatically self-undermining -- a text built on the häften would not conclude that they say nothing -- and B is a reductive 'främst därför att' claim about the collection's value rather than about the guides themselves. A and C then assert mirror-image trends, so one of them is almost certainly the key; deciding between them still requires the passage.

findings.quote: Häftena kan knappast säga något om hur planscherna faktiskt användes i klassrummen.
findings.note: ARGUABLE: the text concedes this claim rather than refuting it. Bråtemo objects “Ett häfte är en önskan, säger han, och ingen vet vad läraren faktiskt sade när dörren var stängd” and the essayist herself grants it: “Det är svårt att komma runt.” The one surviving trace of actual use is null evidence — “I ett enda av dem har en lärare skrivit något i marginalen, och det som står där är ett datum.” Her rebuttal does not reclaim classroom use: “Just därför säger de något, nämligen att förändringen var avsiktlig” — i.e. publisher intent, not what happened behind the closed door. Beatable, not defensible: the case has to stop mid-paragraph at the concession and ignore the “Men bilderna förändras i takt med texterna” turn, and the prompt’s “bäst” delimiter favours key A, which is the essay’s quantified thesis (“andelen frågor sjunker från ungefär två tredjedelar till knappt en tredjedel”; “de sena planscherna har färre småting i utkanterna”). Flagged because A and D are not mutually exclusive — both agree with the text and only centrality separates them.

findings.quote: Det är svårt att komma runt.
findings.note: class 2/6: 'komma runt' in the abstract sense 'get around (an objection)' mirrors English; the settled Swedish idiom for conceding an unavoidable point is 'komma ifrån'. Native alternative: 'Det är svårt att komma ifrån.'

findings.quote: Häftena samlades inte.
findings.note: class 6: the collector sense in Swedish takes the particle -- 'ingen samlade pa haftena'. Bare 'samlades inte' first reads as 'were not gathered/assembled', which is not the intended sense. Native alternative: 'Ingen samlade pa dem.'

findings.quote: Där dominerade beskeden redan i de tidigaste årgångarna, och andelen frågor förblir liten hela vägen.
findings.note: class 6: tense lurch inside one sentence (preterite 'dominerade' + present 'forblir') that an editor would level out to one tense. Native alternative: '... och andelen fragor forblev liten hela vagen.'

findings.quote: it names something the text really does spend room on
findings.note: class 3 (idiom/collocation): “spend room on” is not an English collocation — a blend of “have room for” and “spend time/space on”. Newly rewritten Q1/C rationale text. Editor's rewrite: 'it names something the text really does give room to'.

findings.quote: only one of the readings it allows is the forecast’s fault; the rest are the camera’s
findings.note: class 3 (idiom): new ¶5 prose. A *reading* cannot be a fault — the fault belongs to the cause, not to the interpretation; the sentence silently swaps the two. Editor's rewrite: 'only one of the readings it allows blames the forecast; the rest blame the camera.'

findings.quote: the forecast’s own author points the same way
findings.note: class 3 (collocation): new ¶5 prose. 'point the same way' collocates with evidence, indicators or findings, not with a person. Editor's rewrite: 'and the forecast's own author says as much'.

findings.quote: so a large share of them were made into air that would have produced nothing anyway
findings.note: class 3 (collocation/garden path): 'made into' reads as 'transformed into' before the reader recovers 'flown into'. Editor's rewrite: 'so a large share of them took airplanes down into air that would have produced nothing anyway'.

findings.quote: The layer has “nothing in it to look at” and makes “no cloud of its own”, because
findings.note: class 4 (house style / declared-variety consistency): the passage sets terminal commas and periods INSIDE the closing quote (AmE, 4/4); the rationale layer sets them OUTSIDE (BrE 'logical' style, 10 of 11 instances). The unit declares spelling_variety AmE. Pick one — AmE, to match the passage.

findings.quote: it names something the text really does spend room on
findings.note: class 3 (collocation): 'spend room on' has no native currency; it is 'have room for' crossed with 'spend space/time on'. Editor's rewrite: 'really does spend space on' or 'really does dwell on'.

findings.quote: The reader supplies the join and re-describes the held-in heat as the warming
findings.note: class 1/3 (variety drift): the noun 'join' in the sense of seam/junction is labelled chiefly British; an AmE-declared unit wants 'the connection' or 'the link'. The same sentence then reaches for the gerund ('no second joining'), so the noun is not even carrying its own weight. Editor's rewrite: 'The reader supplies the connection'.

findings.quote: “pull against one another” says that the two oppose, not which of them wins
findings.note: class 2/3 (valency): modern English 'oppose' is transitive; bare intransitive 'the two oppose' is nonstandard and an editor would strike it. Editor's rewrite: 'says that the two are opposed, not which of them wins'.

findings.quote: cannot be answered with a thing the text conspicuously leaves open
findings.note: class 3/4 (idiom/register): 'with a thing' for 'with something' is thin and reads ESL-flavoured in otherwise controlled expository prose. Editor's rewrite: 'cannot be answered with something the text conspicuously leaves open'.

findings.quote: the only depth given is the small hill, and it is not time-of-day dependent
findings.note: class 4 (house style): unhyphenated compound modifier. Editor's rewrite: 'and it does not depend on the time of day'.

findings.quote: He calls the satellite count “the smallest thing those two winters produced”,
findings.note: class 4 (declared-variety consistency): comma outside the closing quote (BrE logical style) while the passage itself punctuates inside the quote (AmE). 10 of 11 rationale instances go BrE, 1 goes AmE, and the unit declares AmE. Normalize to AmE.

findings.quote: it names something the text really does spend room on
findings.note: class 3 (collocation): 'spend room on' is not idiomatic English. Editor's rewrite: 'that the text really does give room to'.

findings.quote: WHY-KEY (C): 141 airplanes were sent through air the forecast had called wet
findings.note: class 4 (house style): sentence opens on a numeral, which magazine style forbids. Editor's rewrite: 'Some 141 airplanes were sent through air the forecast had called wet'.

findings.quote: and the word cool is never used of a contrail
findings.note: class 4 (house style, use vs mention): the word-as-word is unmarked here and in 'Worthless is a word for evidence that says nothing either way', while the same rationales correctly quote “Also” and “pull against one another”. Editor's rewrite: 'and the word “cool” is never used of a contrail'.

findings.quote: many of the descents rather than all of them, and will have bought nothing rather than bought nothing
findings.note: class 4 (typography/clarity): four unmarked mentions in one clause; without quotation marks the contrast is unreadable on first pass. Editor's rewrite: '“many of the descents” rather than “all of them”, and “will have bought nothing” rather than “bought nothing”'.

findings.quote: where he names among the findings that will outlast the trial “that the forecast asks for more descents than the sky calls for”
findings.note: class 2/4 (syntax): 'name' takes a nominal, not a bare that-clause, and the adjunct is wedged between verb and object. Editor's rewrite: 'where he lists, among the findings that will outlast the trial, the fact that the forecast asks for more descents than the sky calls for'.

findings.quote: a forecast asking for more than the sky supplies is the best of those readings
findings.note: class 3 (category slip in paraphrase): a forecast is not a reading. The passage fronts a that-clause ('That the forecast asks for more than the sky supplies is the best of those readings'); the rationale's nominalization loses that and predicates 'reading' of the forecast itself. Editor's rewrite: 'that the forecast asks for more than the sky supplies is the best of those readings'.

findings.quote: and believes the rest would follow. Perhaps it would.
findings.note: class 2 (pronoun number): 'them' (the hundred sensors) governs the sentence, so 'the rest' reads as a countable plural and the echo wants 'Perhaps they would.' Defensible only if 'the rest' is read as a singular remainder. Editor's rewrite: 'Perhaps they would.'

findings.quote: paragraphs 3 to 5, the trial, the audit and the counting, do not touch crystal growth at all
findings.note: class 4 (house style): no serial comma here, but the same rationale uses one two sentences earlier ('cannot see a young contrail, cannot see its height, and cannot tell four or five tracks apart'). Pick one convention.
